EICMA 2026 • Honda Has a Taste of the e-MTB World with the RN0 Motor-Assisted Bicycle
An Icon Resurfaces: The 1987 Boaterhome Is "The First Motorhome for Land and Water," Quite a Sight
37 photos
Photo: UsefulJunk/HeavyDSparks
The word "icon" is being thrown around a lot these days, many times without any actual weight behind it. This is not one of those times: the Boaterhome is an icon if you've ever seen one, a unique vehicle dubbed the world's first motorhome for land and water, luxurious and capable in equal measure, and a true attention magnet.
The Boaterhome is also something of an RV unicorn.
From two different producers, one in the U.S. and the other in Canada, starting with the late 1970s and through to the late 1990s, about 21 units in total were produced. Of these, several remain in various states of disrepair and even fewer are part of private collections.
Then, there's this one: the OG Boaterhome , which is also the most impeccable unit of them all, still functional, still good looking, and as luck would have it (*if you're in the market) ready for a new owner.
Photo: UsefulJunk/HeavyDSparks This is the Boaterhome that became Internet-famous years ago and that has made somewhat of a habit of popping up every now and then, usually when it changes hands. Whenever that happens, it never fails to make headlines, if only because the extra media attention means a better look at a rig of the kind you won't find anywhere else.
Boaterhome is ridiculous looking and ridiculously designed, but it's somehow able to avoid the trap other dual-purpose vehicles fall into. If you think of amphibious vehicles that promise you they'll conquer land and water with ease, grace, and preferably good fuel economy, they never deliver: they're neither good cars nor particularly nice boats.
Boaterhome is both, and that's because it's designed to separate once it hits a body of water. On the road and at camp, it's a nice, family-friendly motorhome with everything you need inside – like, everything, including sleeping for four, a kitchen, and a bathroom. Once you back up into a lake, it becomes a fiberglass, shallow-hull boat.
Photo: UsefulJunk/HeavyDSparks Why now? This rig is a 1987 unit, built with an '87 Ford Econoline van (E-350 series) and an '86 Sport King boat hull. Its odo currently reads a little over 15,000 miles (24,140 km), none of which were put there by the current owner.
That owner is Jason Grossman, who bought it at auction in 2022 from John Ortlieb, who had inherited it from his father, along with a lesser preserved unit. Grossman is also the owner of the Once Upon a Time in America Museum and Smoke Wagon Saloon in Kanab, Utah, which explains why the rig never got any real-life use, since it was put on display for the public.
Photo: Barrett-Jackson While here, the Boaterhome was in excellent company. The Museum also houses the Guinness-certified Midnight Rider limousine and the one-of-one Dobbertin HydroCar , but also unique or rare oddities like Hitler's head X-ray and Lincoln's hat, and a collection of 35+ cars and even more strange vehicles.
Grossman reached out to YouTuber HeavyD, aka David Sparks from the HeavyDSparks channel, to offload some inventory through consignment. Sparks agreed, on the condition that he'd be allowed to take the boat part of the Boaterhome out for a test drive, complete with the inflatable "spinning wheel of death," which Grossman agreed.
The entire test drive was documented on camera for the video at the bottom of the page, as is customary these days. Sparks himself owns a Boaterhome, though his is even rarer, being built on a Dodge chassis, longer, more powerful, but also in poorer condition – so he had a second interest in seeing how this one performed.
Photo: Barrett-Jackson The OG Boaterhome The video and the recent listing offers new insight into the rig, including extra details that were never made public before. That it could accommodate four guests, had a kitchen, and a wet bathroom was common knowledge. So was the fact that the 28-foot (8.5-meter) boat sat on a tandem-axle trailer built into the chassis of the van, or that it drew power from a Mercury Marine 200 hp DFI outboard engine.
Since the last time the Boaterhome made headlines, it's been upgraded and refreshed, to the point where its amenities are now less late-'80s-style and more modern.
Photo: YouTube / Barcroft Cars For instance, the boat section got lithium batteries, a Zantrex charger, and a 3000W inverter, as well as a new 120V AC, a new instant water heater, and a new bilge pump. Features now include a reinforced bulkhead, underwater lights, color-changing LED lights throughout, and a 22-speaker audio system.
It's been painted and re-upholstered. In terms of autonomy, it can hold 55 gallons (208 liters) of fresh water, 25 gallons (94 liters) of gray, and 25 gallons of black water, but also 27 gallons (102 liters) of fuel in a tank on the starboard side, and 35 gallons (132 liters) more in another one on the portside.
The van has also been refreshed , with new paint, new window tint, new upholstery and carpets, new fuel lines, new AC, and a new stereo, among other things.
Photo: UsedCarSite.net The listing mentions the rig is in "vintage excellent" condition, and you can tell this much from the video. Sparks himself confirms the rig runs and drives excellently, with the boat maximum out at 20 mph (32 kph) when loaded with people and gear and 31 mph (50 kph) with just him at the cockpit.
Unlike his unit, this one has a pass-through from the cab to the boat part, which means it can really function as a motorhome.
Photo: Barrett-Jackson The original Boaterhome has 18 bids as of this writing, with the listing recommending a bid range between $69,000 and $89,000. If you're not even thinking about buying it, window shopping costs nothing but half an hour of your (free) time.

source_document.body:
ID 468308872 © Artem Evdokimov | Dreamstime.com
By The Loadstar team
11 November 2026
In recent months, a daily review of container terminal utilisation levels has become something of a ‘must-read’ for supply chain planners seeking to understand where boxes may be delayed, and for how long.
That remains an art rather than science, but indicates how the container shipping industry has experienced something of a paradigm shift into an era in which waves of mega-congestion ripple across the port and shipping system.
Terminal occupancy levels – ie, how many containers are sitting in a yard awaiting either a truck or loading on a vessel – continue to sit way above what these facilities were designed to handle.
A small selection from just today, as reported by Kuehne+Nagel: Tokyo AOM yard density is at 113%, up from 96%; Yokohama is above 100%; Busan’s BNCT is around 95% overall, “with laden density near 100% and heavy-discharge ships at risk of lower priority”; and Rotterdam’s ECT is at 94% yard occupancy.
Some of this is beyond terminal operators’ control – they have no say over when vessels arrive, or how delayed they might have been at the previous port; while wars, weather, and other disruptive events are in the hands of the gods – or people who think of themselves as such…
However, in the spirit of supply chain resilience, they could be far better prepared to tackle congestion when it arises.
Drewry’s recent analysis of container port congestion is actually relatively straightforward: the difference in clearing a terminal that is 85%+ utilised and one that is 70% utilised, is massive – a one-day closure at the latter can be cleared in two days; at the former it will take a week; and if multiple disruptions occur, there is very little chance of the former ever clearing completely.
This has been demonstrated clearly over the past couple of months with the arrival of successive typhoons in key Asia loading ports. The effect this had on vessel departures was, ultimately, congestion elsewhere in the world, because those ports too had been operating at 85%+ utliisation.
Why?
Because, as Drewry’s Eleanor Hadland succinctly put it: “No terminal manager gets rewarded for having empty space.”
In fact, the opposite is true. Terminal operators – especially those which have carriers as sister companies – have enjoyed a bumper 2026, as recent third-quarter results demonstrated.
At the same time, their ultimate customers – cargo owners, their freight forwarders, and finally everyday consumers – face increased costs as they witness supply chains fracturing in front of their eyes.
It doesn’t have to be like this, The Loadstar believes.
Port authorities could future-proof their container terminals – which mostly they ultimately own on a landlord basis – by stipulating in concession contracts that a certain amount of nominal terminal capacity must remain unused, except when disruptions demand it.
Your port needs a further 2m teu of container capacity? Stipulate that the operator builds a terminal with a nominal 2.5m teu capacity, thus giving the container supply chain into the port’s hinterland the buffer this year has so clearly shown is needed.

source_document.body:
Kuehne+Nagel and Amazon have tested a shared charging model that lets Kuehne+Nagel’s electric trucks charge up at Amazon facilities in the UK.
What’s Related
In the pilot, Kuehne+Nagel, which works as a logistics partner to Amazon, got access to existing fast chargers at Amazon sites its trucks already visit. The trucks plugged in while they were being loaded and unloaded, so drivers didn’t have to go out of their way to find a charger.
Kuehne+Nagel said the pilot reached a 90% charging success rate. That number is the share of planned charging stops that ended in a successful session. Trucks also gained 40% in battery charge during their time on site, the company said.
“Our pilot addresses two key challenges: it expands the charging network, which makes it easier to plan electric truck journeys; and it ensures that charging infrastructure is sufficiently utilized to deliver a return on investment,” said John de Dryver, global strategy and sustainability manager at Kuehne+Nagel.
How it works
Charging stations for heavy trucks take a big upfront investment, so they need steady use to make financial sense. Sharing chargers that are already on site at Amazon helps keep them busy. It also gives outside carriers access to fast truck charging, which Kuehne+Nagel called a key barrier to running electric line-haul routes.
Kuehne+Nagel said Amazon’s UK sites made sense for two reasons. First, the chargers are fast. They can typically take a truck battery from 20% to 80% in about 45 minutes, which fits inside a normal loading or unloading window. Second, Kuehne+Nagel trucks already stop at Amazon fulfillment centers regularly, so there were no extra miles involved.
Access to charging still a blocker
Kuehne+Nagel said the range and charging speeds of heavy-duty electric trucks still don’t fully match what day-to-day operations require. It added that reliable access to charging is still a key bottleneck.
“One of the most encouraging findings from the pilot was that the vast majority of unsuccessful charging attempts were not linked to the charging technology or the operational model itself,” said Matthew Scoble, road logistics cross-border specialist at Kuehne+Nagel. “This reinforces our belief that the model we piloted is a viable and scalable solution, with the potential to achieve near 100% charging success rates under normal operating conditions.”

source_document.body:
EICMA 2026 • Yamaha Births New Adventure Scooter Family, Three RW Models That Look More Like Motorcycles
It's Time To Shut Up About Physical Buttons for the Climate Control System. We Don't Need Them.
10 photos
Photo: WheelsAge
There's a Nikki and Bear-level obsession sweeping through the automotive industry and it has everything to do with buttons. Yes, the supposedly indispensable physical buttons and rotary dials that operate your car's climate control system. Apparently, taking these buttons away is nothing short of ergonomic genocide, and media people have been complaining about this for years.
What happened next was pretty predictable. Consumers got in on the action (complaining) and manufacturers started receiving praise for bringing back physical controls, like they rediscovered some type of long-lost technology. And you know what? I used to agree with those complaining about this stuff.
It's easy to argue in favor of physical buttons. They're much easier to locate without you taking your eyes off the road, and the iconic rotary dial is incredibly intuitive. I mean, who would want essential functions buried inside a touchscreen ? Especially when getting to them required more than one click.
But at one point, and this happened recently - I asked myself a surprisingly obvious question: How often do we actually make adjustments to the climate control system while driving?
Seriously, think about it. You get in your car, start the engine, and your preferred temperature is already set. Maybe you need to make a slight adjustment based on outside temperature. Whatever. You set it, and drive off.
If your car has an automatic climate control system, which the vast majority of modern vehicles do, the tech takes care of virtually everything from fan speed to air distribution, temperature regulation and so on. And yet, judging by the endless complaints about touchscreen controls, you'd think the average driver spends half his/her commute desperately adjusting the cabin temperature.
What I'd like to know is who's constantly reaching for the temperature dial every 45 seconds? You guys switching between 70 and 72 degrees at every intersection? Is adjusting the fan speed really an integral part of the driving experience for you? Of course, I know there are exceptions. Sometimes the windshield fogs up and what have you, but none of this stuff is so "mission critical" that it can't wait a few seconds until you stop at the next light.
Photo: WheelsAge And how difficult is it really to change something on your touchscreen? It's a simple tap. It's not like you need to put in your pin code or solve one of those impossible "prove that you're human" image prompts. I know that you might need to glance at the screen, but like I said, it's not an emergency. It can wait until the next light.
Or if you're on the highway, your modern car will already have some type of self-driving feature. Activate that, and then you can intermittently take your eyes off the road for a split second to tap a screen.
Or better yet, use voice commands. It's a little slower than turning a dial, but again, who cares? You're not taking your eyes off the road at all. Modern cars allow you to adjust temperature inside simply by telling them you're cold. You don't even need to specify an exact temperature, even though you obviously can.
Now, before you call me some type of touchscreen Nazi, let me just say that I don't think we should eliminate every physical button or control from the cabin. That's not what I'm saying. Because some controls genuinely benefit from a more hands-on approach.
Volume, for example. Give me a proper knob any day. Or at least physical steering wheel controls . Because volume is something you actually adjust several times per day, unlike temperature. We obviously should keep the turn signal stalk as well, duh. And windshield wipers? Same story. Hazard lights, too. Umm, and maybe the defroster? But I'm not 100% here because it works just as well on a screen as long as it's permanently displayed.
Photo: WheelsAge You guys picking up what I'm putting down? These controls directly impact the driver's ability to operate the vehicle safely. Changing the cabin temperature by 2 degrees does not. It doesn't even belong in the same conversation. Physical buttons for the climate control system... please. I think we can move on, don't you?
Now, none of this means that carmakers should get a free pass for awful touchscreen interfaces. Nobody wants a vital function buried several menus deep.
But at the same time, we need to let manufacturers innovate. Because remember, nobody thought a clamshell mobile phone was a good idea in the first place, and then the original Motorola RAZR became a global best-seller. Same goes for cell phones with cameras. Who would want a camera embedded into their phone? Turns out, everyone!
In conclusion, let's see what else they come up with going forward. We can criticize exterior and interior designs all we want, but when it comes to tech, we're either moving forward or we're standing still. And standing still is the equivalent of going backwards.
Feel free to let me know how you guys feel about this. Don't hold back.

source_document.body:
Every few years, I apparently feel compelled to remind Honda that it is sitting on what could be one of the easiest home runs in the electric motorcycle industry: just make an electric Super Cub already.
I’m not talking about an electric scooter vaguely inspired by the Super Cub. Not another futuristic concept with swoopy bodywork and a name that looks like a Wi-Fi password. I mean an actual honest-to-goodness Honda Super Cub, except electric.
The formula is already sitting right there.
The Honda Super Cub is arguably the most successful motor vehicle ever created, with well over 100 million produced since its introduction in 1958. It’s still in continuous production today.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
And a huge part of that success comes down to how approachable the thing is. It isn’t supposed to be intimidating, excessively powerful, or particularly complicated. It’s simple, practical transportation wrapped in one of the most recognizable two-wheeler designs ever created.
In other words, it’s practically begging to become electric.
The beauty of the bike is how simple and timeless it is, with the appearance barely changing in nearly 7 decades. And with the design freedom that electric drivetrains provide, upgrading the cute little bike to an electric future would be a walk in the park for Honda’s engineers.
An in-wheel motor would be a simple, cheap solution that frees up even more space in the body for batteries.
And Honda wouldn’t need some enormous battery capable of highway touring. Give an electric Super Cub enough battery for perhaps 50-60 miles (80-95 km) of real-world urban riding, a motor capable of roughly 50-60 mph (80-95 km/h), and simple Level 1 charging from a normal wall outlet. As a city runabout or a beachside cruiser, those middle-of-the-road specs would be perfect.
Even better, make the battery removable. Honda already has its Mobile Power Pack e: swappable battery system used in various electric two-wheelers, and an electric Super Cub would be an incredible platform to expand it.
The resulting bike could hit an unusually sweet spot.
The Honda EV Cub concept unveiled 10 years ago and subsequently abandoned
There are millions of people riding electric bicycles today who will eventually want something faster , but don’t necessarily want a 500-pound (220 kg) electric motorcycle capable of hitting 120 mph (200 km/h). An electric Super Cub would be a natural next step: light, unintimidating, easy to ride, cheap to operate, and fast enough to actually function as a real urban vehicle.
It would also be one of the rare electric motorcycles that could appeal to people who aren’t necessarily looking for an “electric motorcycle.” An electric version is in such high demand that companies specialize in retrofit kits to convert classic Cubs into EVs.
The Super Cub already has decades of cultural cachet. It’s cute. It’s useful. It’s nostalgic without feeling ancient. It’s the kind of motorcycle that can appeal equally to a lifelong rider and someone who has never considered owning a motorcycle before.
And perhaps most importantly, Honda could actually sell the thing globally. The same basic electric Super Cub could work in dense European cities, throughout Asia, and in American cities and suburbs. It doesn’t need to win spec-sheet battles. It just needs to be affordable, reliable, and unmistakably a Super Cub.
Honda has already shown that it understands the importance of electrifying small two-wheelers. It’s even made a token gesture with a Cub-like e-scooter in China . But there’s a difference between making another electric scooter and electrifying perhaps the most famous small motorcycle ever made.
So here I am once again, Honda.
You’ve got the name. You’ve got the design. You’ve got the batteries. You’ve got the manufacturing scale.
Just put all the pieces together and give us the electric Super Cub already. The world is waiting, and will thank you.

source_document.body:
A U.S. Army Soldier assigned to 3rd Squadron, 278th Armored Cavalry Regiment, Task Force Reaper, refuels a M1A3 SEP V3 Abrams tank after participating in a live-fire exercise in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility, Feb. 11, 2026. Tactical refueling is an essential component of combat logistics support in contested environments and extends operational reach and capabilities on the battlefield. (U.S. Army photo by Joseph Kumzak)
As supply lines and communications networks become priority targets for adversaries, building logistics capabilities that can move personnel and materiel safely and effectively will be critical to military efforts.
Doing so requires building a digital infrastructure that can enable technologies such as software-defined systems, smart warehousing and remote updates, allowing logisticians and troops in the field to work through contested environments to successfully carry out missions.
In a recent webinar , Breaking Defense examined these challenges with Matthew Constanzi, lead for the C5ISR Center’s Sustainment Transformation Predictive Logistics Team at Army DEVCOM; Josh Wallin and Carlton Haelig, fellows at the Defense Program for the Center for a New American Security; and Mike Zizza, sales and growth leader for Wind RiverX.
“The biggest challenge that I’ve seen from my position is the Army’s ability to execute what some will term precision logistics, and that’s just being able to provide the accurate amount of supplies that you need across the battlefield,” said Costanzi, “and doing that in dispersed and communication-denied and degraded environments.
“Within that challenge itself, it really boils down to the ability for the Army to be able to capture accurate and timely tactical-level logistics asset information from both assets and commodities on the battlefield.”
Building the communications and logistics backbones needed to meet that precision logistics challenge requires accurate and timely data, software-driven capabilities and dependable communications networks.
A Hunter Wolf unmanned ground vehicle assigned to Charlie Battery, 3rd Battalion, 320th Field Artillery Regiment, 3rd Mobile Brigade, 101st Airborne Division (Air Assault), transports cargo during a training exercise at the Joint Readiness Training Center, Fort Polk, Louisiana, April 13, 2026. The Hunter Wolf platform, selected for the U.S. Army’s Small Multipurpose Equipment Transport (S-MET) program, is designed to enhance Soldier mobility and mission endurance by automating logistics and providing tactical support in contested environments. (U.S. Army photo by Spc. Mariam Diallo)
Using data, not drowning in it
Logistics efforts in contested environments start with reliable, usable data. While sensor networks collect vast amounts of data, there is a difference between data and usable data. Without tools to sort through reams of data and make it digestible for those who need to use it, forces run the risk of drowning in information that they can’t effectively make sense of.
“There is a human capital aspect to it,” said Haelig. “By aggregating all of this data, you also present a challenge where folks might raise a question and say, ‘How do we make sense of this? How do we know that this data is accurate? How do we know that it’s the appropriate data for whatever it is we’re trying to get done?’
“And you have to sell it to the actual operators, whether they’re civilians or uniformed operators, that this is going to make their job easier, it is going to make these processes more effective; and you also have to give them the tools to do so.”
Software helps meet this challenge, and artificial intelligence (AI) is already offering ways to help manage data, with those capabilities only expected to grow as AI becomes more effective at sorting through massive datasets to provide usable data. Putting those tools into the hands of both rear-guard logisticians and frontline troops offers the ability to quickly and accurately identify key elements such as open logistics routes, potential areas that may be contested or denied and alternate wayfinding capabilities for both crewed and uncrewed delivery platforms.
Costanzi pointed out that the C5ISR Center is already working on these tools. The center has a proof of concept that it is testing to capture bulk information from fuelers and mobile fuel storage and distribution units, move that data autonomously into command and control (C2) nodes, then push it into the Army data fabric so it can be used by sustainment planners and other warfighting applications. The center is also working with the armaments and soldier Centers to track ammunition from its initial procurement to its consumption rates in the field.
“The big heavy hitters of the Army today are fuel and ammunition, so tracking those and knowing what is at each echelon so that you can provide resupply in a more precision manner definitely is key,” he said.
Quantity of data matters, but quality matters much more, and building tools to help take some of the cognitive burden off of operators will be critical to effective logistics, said Wallin.
“Being able to do things like automatic prediction, making recommendations – even things like filling out supply orders automatically – that’s where we see some potential benefit here,” he said. “Those are things that hopefully can avoid having human operators just being overwhelmed by the amount of information that’s coming in. It’s not just getting more information in, it’s having the tools in place so that operators are actually able to process it.”
Software-driven logistics
The fundamental question of logistics is how to get people and materiel from Point A to Point B safely and efficiently. The answers to that question will vary widely based on region – using highway networks in Europe is a far different logistical challenge than island-hopping in the Pacific – but when logistics are needed in contested environments, the key considerations include identifying usable alternate routes and protecting assets from confiscation or attacks. Being able to use software to help identify and mitigate those challenges speeds up the process and allows for rapid adaptation when necessary.
The Army’s Next-Generation Command and Control (NGC2) effort is driving implementation of software capabilities for logistics. Much of the Army’s logistics efforts still run on paper, but NGC2 aims to build a software structure that will modernize logistics through methods such as digitizing Preventive Maintenance Checks and Services (PCMS), AI-assisted technical manual navigation, troubleshooting, reporting and even capabilities such as medical evacuations.
“All that reporting was done in either spreadsheets or across a couple different enterprise systems, if there even was an enterprise system,” said Costanzi. “They’re trying to pull all that together into basically a sustainment planning tool, planning and execution tool under that NGC2 umbrella.”
Automating these processes not only takes some of the workload off of human operators, but also helps streamline data collection and evaluation. If a logistician has to manually track replacement parts, there is the potential for inaccurate counting, outdated information about stockpiles or data-entry duplication, raising the risk of old or wrong data giving a false picture of materiel on hand. And as assets move around, accurately tracking what assets are where – along with all of their necessary supplements such as replacement parts, fuel and ammunition – is critical to developing a true understanding of supplies on hand, resupply needs and readiness.
“All of that begins with these kinds of uncontested, peacetime software solutions, and from what I understand, these are being exercised in these types of operational environments, and these pitfalls and gaps are being raised as issues,” said Haelig. “But you can’t lose sight of the contested part of the contested logistics problem.”
Software and initiatives such as NGC2 will help solve – or are beginning to solve – some of these challenges, but as Zizza points out, NGC2 will also include legacy systems that are already in the field, and any software solution will have to be functional on the edge to be a truly effective logistics tool.
“The core of that is the idea of software being the real backbone of these systems, and systems of systems that are living code that can be modernized and updated,” said Zizza. “You could argue that contested logistics is ultimately a software resilience problem as much as a physical one, as much as one that’s challenged by weather and extreme distances like in places like the Pacific. When looking at software, being responsive equals survivability, and that equals readiness.”
The importance of reliable communications
Logistics networks run on dependable communications, and in contested environments existing networks may not be easy to access or may not be available at all. In many cases, US forces will be required to bring the network with them or adapt to communications infrastructure such as private 5G networks.
But as logistics tools become increasingly cloud-based, data connectivity increases in importance, and must be maintained to allow forces to communicate and effectively move assets where they need to be. The US and its allies will need to be able to implement communications capability at every level, so that even if they cannot connect to the upper echelon, frontline tactical units will still be able to share information and communicate with each other.
“You need to have really good resilience in your network, and it’s not just resilience in the sense of being able to keep all of your logistics nodes connected at all times, it’s being able to gracefully degrade,” said Wallin. “It’s accepting the fact that when you’re up against a very capable adversary, it is likely that you’re going to lose some nodes. That could be digitally, so it could be you lose communications; it could be physically, meaning you simply don’t have access to certain places because they’re being held under threat.
Costanzi echoed that concern, with the added note that forces in the field will not always have access to the same kinds of communications networks that vendors or planners have available to them as they are designing and testing logistics tools.
“All these vendors are working off of high-speed data connections, and I don’t know that we’re always going to see that in the field,” said Costanzi. “We need to make sure that we have ways to pare our data down smaller to be able to work in those degraded environments, or we’re going to end up fighting blind.”
